scores.note: It would be the biggest laugh, but the smear is a cartoon blob of paint with drips, not light. The camera snaps home in about 0.17 s, and for a few frames she sits as a flat cut-out with no ring before she pops back.

The pressed glossy oval with its eye-streak is the best splat picture, and Ava's double-take ends it well. The rush-in frames are an unreadable pink tongue that fills the screen, and the smear leaves through the bottom of the frame.

The cleanest graphic of the three (her outline and ring stamped in light, with a smooth cross-fade home), but the impact is a three-frame grey wash over the whole screen. Like the other two, it needs a huge camera dive and only works for panels that push south.

All of it plays from the home camera, so the overshoot, the teeter at the brink and the reel back up her trail read at TV size, and the arm of glass sleeves is pure Lumen. The 'she has already landed' pause (about 0.15 s) and the rewind (about 0.2 s) are too short to register.

The best acting of the rewinds, and the low Dutch angle is dramatic. But the camera leaves the board for over a second, both name tags disappear and pop back, Ava blooms into a white blob, and the whip home takes about 4 frames.

The white ring that marks her real space helps, but the scene goes murky and the low shot hard-cuts back to the board in one frame. During the rewind, the trail spooling back reads as a pink blob under her.

The warm three-stroke bird is the most Lumen of the cuckoos. The camera stays close for the whole act, so Ava is cropped to a glowing blob in the corner, and the bobs are too small to count from the couch.

The most readable cuckoo: the camera stays near home, the big bird of light sits on a stick with sound arcs for each call, and the annoyed Maya, the peck and the slide are all clear. The bird pops in fully formed in one frame with no door opening first, and Maya's name tag blinks off and back on.

Showing the register as tally marks crossed by a slash is clever, but the bird blooms into a scribble nobody can read and the little house looks like a 'home' icon from a UI. The house and tally stay on the board for a few frames after the camera is home.

A lit tray of smoked glass with bright edges is Lumen's own material and reads at a glance, and the whip back (2 frames and a ring) lands cleanly with her on the right space. The gag is quieter than its description: the jolt and the rocking barely show.
The long-exposure streak sits right where the tray was, so the freeze reads as 'paused on the tray' instead of 'hanging over nothing'. The desaturation is a CSS filter laid over the whole picture.

Beautiful and calm from the home camera, with real light through a crack and her shadow cut out of it, so the dark lane points the way she drifts. The light reads as two headlight beams more than as one wedge, and the door fin covers part of Maya's name tag ('AYA').
Maya basking like a cat in the sun is charming, but the crack is drawn as a hollow rectangle floating above the wall and her long shadow is a hard-edged dark strip. Ava's highlight blows out.

The most finished entry: the room's light sinks, a slab of warm light stands up behind the panel, and a clean wedge with motes carries her one space. The door then closes to a line and goes out, leaving nothing behind; it is calm, readable from the couch, and works for any wall.

winner.why: It is the one entry built entirely from Lumen's own light, glass and darkness, with no camera stunt and no glitch, and the wedge of light points the way she will go before she moves, so the room reads the push without words. Taking away the plate and showing a brighter room behind the wall is a real surprise, and it turns an occasional shove into a quiet moment of wonder that will still be lovely the fifth time it plays.
winner.port: Create the warm SpotLight in scene.js at load time with intensity 0: adding a light at runtime makes three.js recompile every lit material, which causes a hitch the first time a panel fires. When several panels fire in one register, share one arena.dim dip with no stacking and restore it exactly. Keep the camera home or shrink the drift, because the real board is 10-13 wide with a HUD over the bottom 40%. Keep the pushed robot's name tag at full brightness and clear of the door slab, which currently glows over it. Test all four push directions and inner walls: a standing slab mid-board can hide robots behind it, the wedge must clip at walls and the board edge, and a pushed line of robots must drift together. It runs 1.77 s of the 2 s budget, and the door must be shut before the next move starts.

runner_up.why: It is the comic version that never leaves the home camera, so the overshoot, the teeter at the brink and the rewind up her own trail all read at TV size, and the telescoping arm of glass and light belongs in Lumen. Going off the edge really costs a reboot, so the room gasps before the board takes it back and they laugh.
runner_up.port: When the panel fires, plan the overshoot from the board: up to 2 empty spaces, stopping before robots and walls, ending at the brink only when an edge or pit is in reach. Check that the no-room fallback (a guilty extra clack in place) still lands, and never let the overshoot cross a belt, checkpoint or battery it could seem to trigger. Lengthen the 'landed' pause to about 0.3 s and the rewind to about 0.35 s, taking the time from the arm's retraction, since it already runs 1.97 s of the 2 s budget. The rewind must reel in the game's own trail (bot.trail) and leave it exactly as a one-space push would.
